title: Advantages and Limitations of AI
subtopics: Dependence on context and data quality
Why AI should not automatically be trusted
learning_outcomes: Explain advantages and Limitations of AI and connect at least two of its listed subtopics.
Apply the central idea in advantages and Limitations of AI to a small example or select a suitable approach for a stated scenario.
Identify an important assumption, failure mode, risk, or limitation and describe how it should be checked.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study advantages and Limitations of AI within Introduction to Artificial Intelligence. You will connect the syllabus topics below to a small, inspectable example and practice stating what the evidence does—and does not—support.
content.why_it_matters: AI literacy begins with the task and the people affected by it. Treat an AI output as a proposal to inspect, not as automatic proof.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: AI can scale repetitive analysis and identify patterns, but results depend on data quality, context, distribution, and infrastructure. Reliability must be measured on representative cases, and high-impact outputs need suitable oversight.

content_blocks.title: Syllabus topics covered in this lesson

items.title: Speed and scalability
items.text: Speed and scalability is one of the concepts used to reason about advantages and limitations of ai. Define the inputs, assumptions, and intended result in this context, then test the idea on a small representative example and document where it may not apply.

items.title: Consistency and automation
items.text: Automation follows a defined workflow; AI may add learned predictions, perception, ranking, or generated candidates. Compare the AI approach with a simpler rule-based or manual baseline before adding complexity.

items.title: Data requirements and infrastructure costs

items.title: Dependence on context and data quality
items.text: Data quality includes accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, and fitness for the intended task. Clean-looking records can still fail to represent the target population or real deployment conditions.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: 1. Identify what advantages and limitations of ai takes as input and what result or decision it is intended to support. 2. Read the example before running it and predict the output. 3. Run the small example, compare actual and expected output, then change one input or assumption and repeat. 4. Record what the example demonstrates and what it does not demonstrate about a real system.

content_blocks.title: A practical way to reason about it
content_blocks.text: Start with the task definition and the inputs available. Make the expected behavior explicit, choose a simple reference point, and inspect both ordinary examples and cases where assumptions may fail. AI literacy begins with the task and the people affected by it. Treat an AI output as a proposal to inspect, not as automatic proof.

content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original snippet or return to the small synthetic input, rerun it, and change one value at a time. Do not add real credentials, private user data, or untrusted code to the example.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: If the output differs, check indentation and spelling, confirm you saved the intended file, and compare each input value with the example. If the example runs as expected, do not infer that it proves a trained model works; this snippet is a deterministic teaching aid. Keep sensitive data out of tests.

content_blocks.title: Check before you trust a result
content_blocks.text: This is a small, deterministic teaching example—not a trained AI model or evidence of production performance. Run it with a local Python 3 interpreter; do not paste secrets or private data into experiments.

content_blocks.title: Recap and next step
content_blocks.text: Recap: AI can scale repetitive analysis and identify patterns, but results depend on data quality, context, distribution, and infrastructure. Reliability must be measured on representative cases, and high-impact outputs need suitable oversight. Next, connect this lesson to its prerequisite or next lesson and carry the same habit forward: define success, test a representative case, inspect failures, and document limitations.

content.task: Try it yourself: take five example systems related to advantages and limitations of ai. Classify each by its task, input, output, and AI approach; justify one ambiguous case and state evidence that would change your classification.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the core concept and accurately refer to the source syllabus topics.
Record a prediction and compare it with a reproducible result or a clearly stated manual trace.
Document at least one limitation, safety consideration, or evaluation requirement.
hints: Write down the inputs, expected output, and assumptions before changing the example.
Change only one input or condition and compare the results with your original prediction.
Ask whether the example covers realistic cases, important subgroups, and failure conditions; a toy example does not establish production reliability.
